goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — Read-modify-save loses match_count increments when concurrent validations match the same address.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17 a classic read-modify-write pattern: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a race condition - if two concurrent requests validate the same blocked email address, both read the same match_count value, increment it locally, and save, resulting in only one increment being persisted instead of two. This is a real concurrency bug in the newly introduced code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — The prototype-level mutable array shares rejected addresses across controller instances instead of resetting per signup form.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` being added at line 17 as a property on the controller definition. In Ember.js, when you define a mutable object (like an array) directly on the prototype like this, it becomes shared across all instances of the controller. This means if one user's signup form adds an email to rejectedEmails, it would persist and affect other controller instances. The correct pattern would be to initialize this in an init() method or use a computed property that returns a new array. This is a real bug in the Ember.js code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:1 — Populating a previously empty historical migration means databases that already recorded this version will never create blocked_emails.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims this is 'populating a previously empty historical migration', but the diff shows this is a NEW migration file being created (indicated by 'new file mode' in the diff header). This is not modifying an existing migration - it's creating a new one. New migrations are designed to be run on databases that don't have them yet, which is the normal Rails migration workflow. The finding misreads what the diff is doing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — The predicate-named should_block? method also persists match statistics, coupling a policy query to a surprising write side effect.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the `should_block?` method in the diff (lines 11-18 of blocked_email.rb) both answers a query ('should this email be blocked?') and performs a write operation (incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at). This is a legitimate design concern - the method name suggests a pure predicate but has side effects. This is a valid architectural/design issue introduced by this diff, not a bug but a real code quality concern that could lead to unexpected behavior when callers assume the method is side-effect-free.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168 — Calling valid? before save runs the new blocked-email SELECT and matching-row UPDATE twice for every signup attempt, doubling attacker-controlled database work.

adjudication.rationale: The diff at app/controllers/users_controller.rb lines 194-200 shows only the error response handling in the `create` action. There is no evidence in the diff of calling `valid?` before `save` - the diff only shows the JSON response being modified to include additional error information. The finding references behavior (double validation) that cannot be verified from the diff shown. The `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is called from the EmailValidator during model validation, but there's no indication in the diff that validation runs twice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Persisting match statistics inside validation counts each signup twice because the controller calls both `valid?` and `save`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 increments `match_count` and updates `last_match_at` every time it's called during validation. In Rails, when creating a record, `valid?` is typically called before `save`, and `save` also runs validations. This means the statistics would be incremented multiple times for a single signup attempt. The diff shows the validator is used via `validates :email, email: true` in user.rb, and the controller in users_controller.rb creates users. This is a legitimate bug where match statistics are inflated due to validation being called multiple times.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — The read-modify-save counter update loses increments when concurrent requests match the same blocked email.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17 a classic read-modify-save pattern: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a race condition - if two concurrent requests match the same blocked email, both read the same match_count value, increment it locally, and save, resulting in only one increment being persisted instead of two. This is a real concurrency bug in the newly introduced code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — Exact case-sensitive lookup lets a blocked signup email bypass the denylist by changing letter case.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows BlockedEmail.should_block? uses an exact match query: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. This is a case-sensitive lookup in most databases. If a user registers with 'Block@spamfromhome.org' but the blocked_emails table contains 'block@spamfromhome.org', the query won't match and the block will be bypassed. Email addresses are case-insensitive by RFC standards, so this is a real security bypass vulnerability in the newly introduced blocking feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:12 — The validator specs stub the blocked-email decision, so they never verify that a persisted blocked address makes a real User validation fail.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the EmailValidator spec at line 12 uses stubs (BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?)) rather than testing with actual persisted BlockedEmail records. While the blocked_email_spec.rb does test the BlockedEmail.should_block? method with real records, and the email_validator_spec.rb tests the validator's behavior when should_block? returns true/false, there is no integration test that verifies the full flow from a persisted BlockedEmail record through to User validation failure. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for the new functionality being added.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — No client test covers caching a server-rejected email and disabling resubmission, so the new blocked-user flow can regress silently.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-side logic at lines 271-274 that caches rejected emails and prevents resubmission. This is nontrivial functionality (pushObject to rejectedEmails array, which triggers the emailValidation computed property via 'rejectedEmails.@each'). The finding correctly identifies that no client-side test is included in this diff for this new behavior - the only tests added are Ruby specs for BlockedEmail model and EmailValidator. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for new functionality.
